content.title: About
content.content: Light butter is a reduced‑fat butter (usually 10‑15 % fat). It is made from cream where a portion of the butterfat is removed, then the remaining fat is blended with water and sometimes a small amount of vegetable oil to improve texture. Light butter retains a buttery taste while providing fewer calories and less saturated fat than regular butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light butter is popular in dietetic cooking where lower calorie content is desired.
Its fat content is typically 10‑15 %, compared with about 80 % in regular butter.
Emulsifiers and stabilizers are often added to maintain a smooth, spreadable texture.
It can be produced from cow’s or goat’s cream.
In some markets it is sold under names like “light butter” or “low‑calorie butter.”

items.title: Reduced saturated fat intake
items.content: The lower fat content helps decrease overall saturated fat consumption, which may positively affect cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and D
items.content: Like regular butter, light butter provides fat‑soluble vitamins A and D important for vision, immunity, and bone health.

items.title: Lower calorie density
items.content: Light butter provides roughly 150‑180 kcal per 100 g, considerably less than traditional butter (~720 kcal).

items.title: Contains conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
items.content: A small amount of CLA remains in light butter and may have beneficial metabolic effects.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Light butter contains milk proteins that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Emulsifiers, stabilizers, and small amounts of vegetable oils may be present, which some diets avoid.

items.title: May not fully replace regular butter in baking
items.content: Reduced fat can affect dough structure, so recipe adjustments may be needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use light butter for spreading on bread, making sauces, sautéing over medium heat, and baking when you want to cut calories. It can be combined with regular butter to achieve desired texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store light butter in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. For long‑term storage it can be frozen at –18 °C, though texture may change after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: Pfeffernusse are traditional German ginger spice cookies, small round biscuits glazed with sugar. They have a slightly crunchy edge and a soft, aromatic interior, flavored with ginger, cinnamon, clove and sometimes a hint of pepper.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pfeffernusse are traditionally baked in the weeks leading up to Christmas and often given as holiday gifts.
The name comes from the German words “Pfeffer” (pepper) and “Nusse” (nut), although the recipe usually contains no nuts.
The recipe dates back to the 16th‑17th centuries, when spices were a luxury item.
Original versions use ground ginger, cinnamon, clove, cardamom and occasionally ground black pepper.
In some regions the cookies are finished with a thin sugar glaze and sometimes sprinkled with chopped nuts.

items.title: Rich in spices
items.content: Ginger and cinnamon have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties that can support immune health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The spice blend provides small amounts of iron, magnesium and manganese.

items.title: Moderate sugar content
items.content: Small servings deliver quick energy without excessive sugar overload.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to ginger, cinnamon or clove.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: People with diabetes should monitor portion size due to the added sugar.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, the cookies are calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pfeffernusse can be enjoyed as a snack, served with tea or coffee, used as decorative toppings for cakes and cupcakes, or crumbled into ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to preserve their crisp texture and spice aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: Rum Ball Cookie is a soft, no‑bake treat made from crushed cookies, cocoa, nuts and aromatic rum, bound together with cream cheese. The result is a melt‑in‑your‑mouth ball with a subtle boozy note, perfect for festive occasions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rum‑ball tradition started in the United States in the mid‑20th century as a quick, no‑bake dessert.
Dark rum is commonly used for its deep flavor, but any aromatic liqueur can be substituted.
Balls are rolled in cocoa powder, shredded coconut, or chopped nuts, adding texture variety.
Because they are not baked, the recipe preserves maximum aroma and texture contrast.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and fat provide a quick energy boost, making them a handy snack.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Cocoa powder is rich in flavonoids, which may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Minerals from nuts
items.content: Nuts supply magnesium, zinc and heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Nut and dairy allergies
items.content: The recipe often includes nuts and cream cheese, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Rum retains a small amount of alcohol; while generally safe in modest amounts, consider children and pregnant individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Sugar and fat make the treat calorie‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled, dusted with cocoa powder or coconut. Ideal as a post‑meal dessert, tea accompaniment, or party treat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 1 month, wrapped in plastic film.

content.title: About
content.content: Croutons are toasted pieces of bread, usually baked or fried until golden and crunchy. They can be made from any type of bread and are often seasoned with oil, herbs, or spices, giving them a flavorful, crisp texture. Croutons are commonly used as a snack, garnish for salads, soups, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croutons originated in medieval Europe as a way to preserve stale bread.
There are many varieties: garlic, cheese, herb‑infused, or sweet versions with cinnamon and sugar.
In Italy similar pieces are called “crostini,” while in France they are known as “croûtons.”
Croutons can be made from white, whole‑grain, or rye bread.
In some cuisines croutons are served with aioli or used as breadcrumbs in casseroles.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Croutons provide quickly digestible carbs that supply energy.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: When made from whole‑grain bread, croutons can contribute dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread base supplies B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Croutons may provide iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, especially if the bread is fortified.

items.title: Enhances meals
items.content: The crunchy texture adds sensory appeal to dishes, encouraging more balanced eating.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Croutons are often salted; excessive sodium intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Because oil is used in preparation, croutons can be calorie‑dense and should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Croutons made from wheat bread contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Repeated frying of oil can create trans fats, which are best avoided.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Croutons can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, soups, stews, or used as a coating for meat and fish. They also pair well with dips such as hummus or guacamole.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store croutons in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the oil from going rancid.

infant-formula-enfamil-infant-powder-mad.title: Enfamil Infant, powder, made with baby water

content.title: About
content.content: Enfamil Infant is a powdered infant formula designed for babies from birth to 12 months. It provides all essential nutrients—including proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals—and is prepared with specially treated baby water (336 ml) for optimal dissolution.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The formula is enriched with DHA and ARA, fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
Contains the prebiotic GOS to support a healthy gut microbiome.
Manufactured under ISO 22000 international quality standards.
Each package includes precise preparation instructions with exact water‑to‑powder ratios.
Clinically tested to confirm safety and efficacy for infants.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: A balanced blend of proteins, fats, and carbohydrates supplies energy and building blocks for the growing body.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA aid in forming neural connections and visual function.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: The prebiotic GOS promotes beneficial bacteria, improving digestion.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, D and zinc help maintain the immune system.

items.title: Optimal hydration
items.content: Specially treated baby water provides the right electrolyte balance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Infants with known cow‑milk protein allergy may react to the formula.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: Too concentrated or too diluted a mixture can lead to dehydration or excess calorie intake.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: Powder can absorb moisture, causing clumping and loss of quality.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Use before the printed expiration date; nutrient quality may decline afterward.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with 336 ml of warm (not hot) baby water. Stir thoroughly until smooth, let it cool to body temperature, and feed the baby immediately.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the container tightly sealed in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 30 days and follow the storage guidelines on the label.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin with raisins is a soft baked good made from wheat flour, eggs, milk, butter, and sugar, with raisins added for sweetness and texture. It has a light vanilla aroma, a subtle raisin flavor, and a tender, slightly moist crumb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Muffins originated in England in the 19th century as a quick way to use leftover batter.
Raisins not only add sweetness but also retain moisture, keeping the muffin juicy.
Traditionally muffins are baked in paper liners, which make serving and transport easy.
In the United States blueberry muffins are popular, but raisins remain a classic European variant.
Gluten‑free muffin versions exist, using rice or almond flour instead of wheat.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates provide quick energy, making the muffin a convenient snack.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Raisins are rich in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter and raisins supply thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Raisins contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Muffins provide iron, potassium, and magnesium, contributing to overall nutrition.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Raisins and added sugar make the muffin calorie‑dense and can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, which is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Butter adds saturated fats; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins with raisins can be enjoyed as a stand‑alone snack, split and spread with cream cheese, added to yogurt, or served to children. Warm muffins are especially aromatic.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or microwave before eating.

ramen-bowl-with-meat-and-egg.title: Ramen bowl with meat and egg

content.title: About
content.content: Ramen bowl with meat and egg is a ready‑to‑eat package of ramen noodles, seasoned meat (usually pork or beef) and a soft‑boiled egg in a flavorful broth. Served in a convenient bowl, it can be heated in the microwave or on the stovetop for a quick lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Japanese ramen often features chashu pork and a half‑soft boiled egg.
Broths come in soy‑based (shoyu), miso, or salt (shio) varieties, each giving a distinct taste.
Ramen started as street food in Japan but has become a popular ready‑meal worldwide.
Eggs are sometimes marinated in soy sauce, giving them a golden hue and rich flavor.
Ramen noodles are made from wheat flour with an alkaline agent (kansui), which gives them a firm, chewy texture.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat and egg provide complete, high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Ramen contains B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Both meat and egg supply heme iron, which aids oxygen transport.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: The broth is often rich in sodium and potassium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of noodles, meat and egg promotes lasting fullness.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Broths can be very salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or gluten
items.content: Ramen noodles contain wheat, and the egg is a common allergen.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Ready‑made meals are often calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Meat safety
items.content: Improper reheating may leave meat undercooked, increasing food‑borne risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the bowl in the microwave (3‑4 minutes) or on the stovetop, stir to distribute the broth evenly. Optionally add fresh vegetables, herbs, soy sauce or chili for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C and consume within 3 days after opening. Freezing is not recommended as the noodles may become mushy.

wonton-dumpling-or-pot-sticker-fried.title: Wonton, dumpling or fried pot sticker

content.title: About
content.content: Wonton is a traditional Asian dish consisting of thinly rolled dough filled with meat, seafood, vegetables, or a combination, then fried until golden. The “pot sticker” version is often served with soy sauce, vinegar, and chili.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wonton originates from Chinese cuisine, but similar items exist in Japan (gyoza) and Korea (mandu).
The dough is made from simple flour and water without leavening, giving it great elasticity.
Fried pot stickers become crispy on the bottom and tender on top thanks to the steam‑fry technique.
Traditional fillings include soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and green onion for flavor depth.
In China, wontons are often served in broth as soup, while in Japan they are popular as fried appetizers.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat, fish or tofu fillings provide complete proteins essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Ingredients such as meat and vegetables contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meaty fillings help maintain hemoglobin levels and prevent anemia.

items.title: Low in carbs in the wrapper
items.content: The thin flour wrapper has fewer carbohydrates than thicker dough products, making wonton moderately caloric.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Vegetable additions (cabbage, carrot, mushrooms) supply antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Allergy to seafood or soy sauce
items.content: Fillings may contain shrimp, fish, or soy sauce, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and some seasonings make the dish high in sodium, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The crispy texture and savory taste can lead to excessive consumption.

items.title: Trans fats from improper frying
items.content: Using old oil or frying at too high a temperature can create trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wontons can be boiled in broth, steamed, or pan‑fried in a small amount of oil until golden. Serve with soy sauce, vinegar, chili oil, or a flavorful broth. They work well as a snack, in salads, or added to soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Raw wontons keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 2‑3 days. Frozen raw wontons last up to 3 months. Fried pot stickers are best eaten within 1‑2 days and should be stored in a dry place to retain crispness.
